body.statement:
Let \(X\) and \(\widetilde X\) be centered Gaussian \(H_n\)-vectors with unit coordinate variances and maximum covariance discrepancy \(\Delta_{m,n}\), and apply the maximum results to their \(2H_n\) signed coordinates.  If \(T=\max_{\ell\le H_n}|X_\ell|\), \(\widetilde T=\max_{\ell\le H_n}|\widetilde X_\ell|\), and \(\kappa_{m,n}=\mathbb E T\), then, for a universal constant \(C\),
\[
 \sup_x\Pr\{|T-x|\le u\}\le C(\kappa_{m,n}+1)u,\qquad u>0,
\]
and
\[
 d_{m,n}\le
 \min\!\left\{1,C\Delta_{m,n}^{1/3}
 \left[1\vee\log\!\left(\frac{2H_n}{\Delta_{m,n}}\right)\right]^{2/3}\right\},
\]
with the right-hand side interpreted as zero when \(\Delta_{m,n}=0\).  These conclusions do not require \(R_{m,n}\) or \(\widehat R_{m,n}\) to be nonsingular.

source.locator: Theorems 2 and 3, applied to the signed coordinate vector
source.verbatim_statement: Theorem 2 (Comparison of distributions). Suppose that p >= 2 and sigma^Y_jj > 0 for all 1 <= j <= p. Then sup_{x in R} | P(max_{1 <= j <= p} X_j <= x) - P(max_{1 <= j <= p} Y_j <= x) | <= C Delta^{1/3}{(1 vee a_p^2 vee log(1/Delta))}^{1/3} log^{1/3} p, where C > 0 depends only on min_j sigma^Y_jj and max_j sigma^Y_jj (the right side is understood to be 0 when Delta = 0). Moreover, in the worst case, a_p <= sqrt(2 log p), so that sup_{x in R} | P(max_j X_j <= x) - P(max_j Y_j <= x) | <= C' Delta^{1/3}{1 vee log(p/Delta)}^{2/3}, where as before C' > 0 depends only on min_j sigma^Y_jj and max_j sigma^Y_jj. Theorem 3 (Anti-concentration). Let (X_1,...,X_p)^T be a centered Gaussian random vector in R^p with sigma_j^2 := E[X_j^2] > 0 for all 1 <= j <= p. Moreover, let underline sigma := min_j sigma_j, overline sigma := max_j sigma_j, and a_p := E[max_j(X_j/sigma_j)]. (i) If the variances are all equal, namely underline sigma = overline sigma = sigma, then for every epsilon > 0, L(max_j X_j, epsilon) <= 4 epsilon(a_p + 1)/sigma. Comment 5: Versions of Theorem 3 and Corollary 1 continue to hold for max_j |X_j|. To see this, observe that max_j |X_j| = max_{1 <= j <= 2p} X'_j where X'_j = X_j for j=1,...,p and X'_{p+j} = -X_j for j=1,...,p. Hence we may apply Theorem 3 to (X'_1,...,X'_{2p})^T to obtain the desired conclusion.

attestation.note: Directly retrieved the authors' arXiv source for arXiv:1301.4807v4 on 2026-09-14. The relevant source is Theorem 2 (comparison of distributions), Theorem 3(i) (equal-variance anti-concentration), and Comment 5 (signed-coordinate reduction for maxima of moduli). With unit marginal variances and p=2H_n signed coordinates, the constants are universal; no covariance nonsingularity assumption appears.
